q: Which ovarian cell type gives rise to most malignant ovarian tumors?
x: Surface epithelium, the Müllerian-type lining of the ovary and fallopian tube, gives rise to about 90 percent of malignant ovarian tumors, most of them high-grade serous carcinomas in older women.

w.Germ cells: Germ cell tumors are the common ovarian neoplasms of girls and young women, but most are benign dermoids and they make up a small share of cancers.
w.Granulosa cells: Granulosa cell tumors are uncommon estrogen-secreting sex cord-stromal tumors with Call-Exner bodies and an inhibin marker.
w.Theca cells: Theca cells give rise to thecomas, benign estrogen-making stromal tumors that are rare compared with epithelial cancers.
w.Stromal fibroblasts: Stromal fibroblasts give rise to fibromas, benign solid tumors that can cause Meigs syndrome but are never the main source of cancers.

pt.say: The surface epithelium column comes first because it gives rise to most ovarian cancers, mainly in older women with a raised CA-125.

q: Which marker rises with an ovarian tumor that shows Schiller-Duval bodies?
x: Schiller-Duval bodies mark a yolk sac tumor, whose cells imitate the embryonic yolk sac and therefore secrete alpha-fetoprotein (AFP); the marker supports the diagnosis and tracks the response to treatment.

w.hCG: hCG comes from trophoblast and marks choriocarcinoma, which shows sheets of trophoblast without villi rather than glomerulus-like bodies.
w.LDH: LDH is the marker of dysgerminoma, the clear-cell germ cell tumor that mirrors seminoma of the testis.
w.Inhibin: Inhibin is secreted by granulosa cells and follows granulosa cell tumors, which show Call-Exner bodies instead.
w.CA-125: CA-125 follows epithelial cancers such as high-grade serous carcinoma and is raised by many benign pelvic conditions.

pt.say: In the germ cell column, the yolk sac tumor box pairs Schiller-Duval bodies with AFP.

q: Which ovarian tumor shows Call-Exner bodies and coffee-bean nuclei?
x: The granulosa cell tumor forms small follicle-like Call-Exner bodies lined by cells with grooved coffee-bean nuclei; it secretes estrogen and inhibin, causing bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia.

w.Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors form tubules and Leydig cell nests and secrete androgens that virilize.
w.Brenner tumor: Brenner tumors also show coffee-bean nuclei, but in nests of transitional-type epithelium without Call-Exner bodies, and they are usually benign.
w.Dysgerminoma: Dysgerminomas grow as sheets of clear fried-egg cells with lymphocytic septa and raise LDH.
w.Thecoma: Thecomas are made of plump, lipid-laden spindle cells that secrete estrogen but form no follicle-like bodies.

pt.say: The granulosa cell tumor box sits in the sex cord-stromal column, where estrogen and inhibin are its products.

q: Which ovarian tumor causes Meigs syndrome with ascites and a right pleural effusion?
x: An ovarian fibroma, a benign tumor of collagen-producing fibroblasts, can leak fluid that causes ascites and a right pleural effusion; both resolve once the fibroma is removed, which separates Meigs syndrome from cancer.

w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors secrete estrogen and inhibin; their clues are bleeding and Call-Exner bodies rather than effusions that vanish after surgery.
w.Mature cystic teratoma: Mature cystic teratomas contain hair, teeth and sebum and are known for torsion, not for ascites with pleural effusion.
w.Mucinous cystadenoma: Mucinous cystadenomas grow very large and multiloculated; pseudomyxoma peritonei usually comes from the appendix, not from Meigs syndrome.
w.Dysgerminoma: Dysgerminoma is a malignant germ cell tumor of young women with raised LDH; it does not produce the benign effusion syndrome.

pt.say: The fibroma box in the sex cord-stromal column is labeled Meigs syndrome.

q: Which serum marker is most characteristic of dysgerminoma?
x: Dysgerminoma, the ovarian counterpart of seminoma, grows as sheets of clear fried-egg cells and typically raises lactate dehydrogenase; some tumors also contain syncytiotrophoblast that makes a little hCG.

w.Alpha-fetoprotein: AFP marks yolk sac tumors; a pure dysgerminoma does not make it, so a high AFP means another germ cell component.
w.CA-125: CA-125 follows epithelial ovarian cancers and many benign pelvic conditions, not germ cell tumors.
w.Inhibin: Inhibin comes from granulosa cells and follows granulosa cell tumors, which are sex cord-stromal tumors.
w.Carcinoembryonic antigen: Carcinoembryonic antigen rises with mucinous and gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas, including metastases to the ovary, not with dysgerminoma.

pt.say: The dysgerminoma box pairs fried-egg cells with LDH, its lactate dehydrogenase marker.

q: Which ovarian tumor causes hirsutism, a deepening voice and clitoromegaly?
x: The Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, a sex cord-stromal tumor of young women, secretes androgens, so it causes hirsutism, a deeper voice, clitoromegaly and loss of menses; testosterone is high while DHEA-S is normal.

w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors make estrogen, causing precocious puberty in girls and bleeding with endometrial hyperplasia in older women.
w.Fibroma: Fibromas make no hormone; they present as a solid mass, sometimes with ascites and a pleural effusion.
w.Brenner tumor: Brenner tumors are usually benign epithelial tumors of transitional-type cells found incidentally; they rarely produce hormones.
w.Serous cystadenoma: Serous cystadenomas are benign epithelial cysts lined by tubal-type cells and make no hormone.

pt.say: The Sertoli-Leydig box reads androgens and virilization, which explains her hirsutism and deep voice.

q: Where do most high-grade serous carcinomas begin?
x: Most high-grade serous carcinomas start as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in the fimbriated fallopian tube, with an early TP53 mutation; this is why salpingectomy lowers ovarian cancer risk.

w.Ovarian surface epithelium: The ovarian surface was long blamed, but tubes removed from BRCA carriers showed that most of these cancers start in the tube.
w.Endometriotic cysts: Endometriotic cysts give rise to clear cell and endometrioid carcinomas, which follow the slower type I pathway.
w.Ovarian stroma: Ovarian stroma gives rise to sex cord-stromal tumors such as fibroma, thecoma and granulosa cell tumor.
w.Peritoneal mesothelium: Primary peritoneal carcinoma exists, but most serous carcinoma on the peritoneum has spread there from a tubal primary.

pt.say: The high-grade serous box reads tubal origin, meaning the fimbriated fallopian tube, with TP53 and BRCA.

q: Which gene is mutated in nearly all high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas?
x: TP53 is mutated early in nearly all high-grade serous carcinomas, already in the tubal precursor, which explains their unstable genomes and aggressive course; germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants add to it in hereditary cases.

w.KRAS: KRAS mutations drive mucinous tumors and low-grade serous carcinomas, which grow slowly from borderline tumors.
w.BRAF: BRAF mutations mark serous borderline tumors and low-grade serous carcinoma, the type I pathway.
w.PTEN: PTEN loss is typical of endometrioid carcinoma of the ovary and endometrium, often linked to endometriosis.
w.ARID1A: ARID1A loss is typical of clear cell and endometrioid carcinomas arising in endometriosis.

pt.say: The high-grade serous box lists TP53 alongside its tubal origin and the BRCA link.

q: Which ovarian cysts form when hCG is very high, as in a molar pregnancy?
x: Very high hCG stimulates the LH receptors on theca cells, so both ovaries fill with multiloculated theca lutein cysts; they regress once the mole is evacuated or the multiple pregnancy ends.

w.Follicular cysts: Follicular cysts form when a single follicle fails to rupture; they are simple, one-sided and unrelated to hCG.
w.Corpus luteum cysts: A corpus luteum cyst is a single cyst after ovulation that may bleed; it is not driven by very high hCG.
w.Endometriomas: Endometriomas are chocolate cysts of old blood from endometriosis, causing cyclic pain and infertility.
w.Paratubal cysts: Paratubal cysts are embryonic remnants in the broad ligament beside the tube and have nothing to do with hCG.

q: Which vessels are compressed first when an ovary twists on its pedicle?
x: Veins and lymphatics have thin walls and low pressure, so torsion collapses them first while arterial blood still enters; the ovary swells with edema, and early Doppler can still show arterial flow.

w.Ovarian artery: The ovarian artery is occluded late, once venous congestion raises tissue pressure; that step causes hemorrhagic infarction.
w.Uterine artery: The uterine artery supplies the uterus and anastomoses with the ovarian artery but is not the vessel twisted in the infundibulopelvic ligament.
w.Internal iliac artery: The internal iliac artery lies on the pelvic sidewall well away from the twisting ovarian pedicle.
w.Inferior epigastric artery: The inferior epigastric artery runs in the anterior abdominal wall and has no part in the ovarian pedicle.

q: Which protective factor removes the tissue where most serous ovarian cancers start?
x: Salpingectomy removes the fimbriated fallopian tube, where serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma, the precursor of most high-grade serous carcinomas, begins; this is why tubes are removed during other pelvic surgery.

w.Breastfeeding: Breastfeeding lowers risk by suppressing ovulation, but it leaves the tube and its epithelium in place.
w.Oral contraceptive use: Oral contraceptives cut ovarian cancer risk by about half by suppressing ovulation, yet the tubal precursor cells remain.
w.Multiparity: Each pregnancy lowers risk by pausing ovulation for months, but no tissue is removed.
w.Hysterectomy leaving tubes and ovaries: Removing the uterus protects only modestly when the fimbriated tubes, where the cancer starts, stay behind.

q: Which bilateral ovarian tumor of signet-ring cells usually comes from the stomach?
x: A Krukenberg tumor is a metastasis, usually from diffuse gastric cancer, that fills both ovaries with mucin-secreting signet-ring cells in a cellular stroma; bilaterality is the clue to metastasis.

w.Brenner tumor: Brenner tumors are usually benign epithelial tumors of transitional-type nests with coffee-bean nuclei.
w.Mucinous cystadenoma: Primary mucinous cystadenomas are large, cystic and usually one-sided, lined by bland columnar cells rather than signet-ring cells.
w.Dysgerminoma: Dysgerminoma is a primary germ cell tumor of clear cells with lymphocytic septa, mostly in young women.
w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors are primary estrogen-secreting tumors with Call-Exner bodies, not metastases.

pt.say: The Krukenberg tumor box heads the metastases column: signet-ring cells, usually from the stomach.

q: Which transvaginal ultrasound feature suggests an adnexal mass is benign?
x: A thin-walled, anechoic, unilocular cyst without solid tissue or flow is almost always benign, often a functional cyst, so a young woman can be managed expectantly with repeat imaging if it persists.

w.Papillary projection: Papillary projections from the cyst wall are solid tissue that raises the risk of borderline or malignant epithelial tumors.
w.Thick septations: Thick or irregular septations suggest a multilocular neoplasm and increase the chance of malignancy.
w.Solid area with flow: Solid tissue with internal Doppler flow is the most worrying feature and places a mass in a high-risk category.
w.Ascites: Ascites with an adnexal mass suggests peritoneal spread of carcinoma, or rarely a fibroma with Meigs syndrome.

pt.say: The reassuring panel shows a simple cyst with a thin, smooth wall and anechoic fluid, the benign pattern.

q: Which feature separates a borderline ovarian tumor from an ovarian carcinoma?
x: Borderline tumors show epithelial stratification, papillae and atypia but no destructive stromal invasion, so most behave well even with noninvasive peritoneal implants; carcinoma invades the stroma.

w.Epithelial stratification: Stratification of the lining occurs in both borderline tumors and carcinomas, so it cannot separate them.
w.Nuclear atypia: Nuclear atypia is present in borderline tumors as well as carcinomas; its degree helps grade them but does not define invasion.
w.Papillary architecture: Papillae are common to serous borderline tumors and serous carcinomas and say nothing about invasion.
w.Peritoneal implants: Borderline tumors can seed the peritoneum too, although their implants are usually noninvasive.

pt.say: The borderline box in the epithelial column reads no stromal invasion, the feature that separates it from carcinoma.

q: Which symptoms most suggest advanced ovarian carcinoma?
x: Bloating, early satiety and rising abdominal girth come from ascites and omental caking as high-grade serous carcinoma seeds the peritoneum; the symptoms are vague, so most women present at an advanced stage.

w.Sudden severe unilateral pain: Sudden severe one-sided pain with vomiting suggests ovarian torsion or a ruptured cyst rather than carcinoma.
w.Cyclic pelvic pain with menses: Cyclic pain with menses points to endometriosis or an endometrioma, which bleed with each cycle.
w.Fever and cervical motion tenderness: Fever with cervical motion tenderness signals pelvic inflammatory disease or a tubo-ovarian abscess.
w.Hirsutism and voice deepening: Virilization points to an androgen-secreting tumor such as a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, not epithelial cancer.
